case_name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / Arrest & Custodial Rights
ratio_decidendi: Custodial violence, torture, and deaths violate the fundamental right to life with dignity under Article 21. The Supreme Court laid down 11 mandatory procedural safeguards for every arrest and detention to prevent abuses of police power.
key_principles: Arresting officer must display accurate, visible, and clear identification and name tags with designations.
A formal memo of arrest must be prepared at the time of arrest, witnessed by at least one family member or respectable citizen, and countersigned by the arrestee.
The arrestee has the right to have a friend, relative, or person known to him informed of his arrest and location of custody within 8 to 12 hours.
Mandatory medical examination of the arrestee by a trained doctor every 48 hours during detention.
Arrestee is entitled to meet and consult with an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout the interrogation.
currentness_check: Substantively codified by Parliament into the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2008 (Sections 41A, 41B, 41D, 50A, 55A) and reenacted in full under Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Sections 35, 36, 38, 47, 51, 53). Reaffirmed continually across all High Courts and Supreme Court benches as binding constitutional minimum.

case_name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / Police Powers of Arrest
ratio_decidendi: Police officers must not automatically arrest an accused upon registration of a cognizable case punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years. Arrest should be made only after satisfying the specific conditions of necessity under Section 41 CrPC (BNSS Section 35(1)), with reasons recorded in writing in a checklist.
key_principles: Mandatory issuance of Notice of Appearance under Section 41A CrPC (now Section 35(3) BNSS) within 14 days of complaint initiation for offences with punishment up to 7 years.
Police must fill a checklist containing specified sub-clauses of Section 41(1)(b) before effecting an arrest.
Magistrates cannot authorize mechanical detention without reviewing the police officer's recorded reasons for arrest.
Failure to comply with arrest guidelines subjects the arresting officer to departmental action and contempt of court.
currentness_check: Reaffirmed by the Supreme Court in Satender Kumar Antil (2022) 10 SCC 51 and Md. Asfak Alam v. State of Jharkhand (2023). Fully binding under BNSS 2023 Section 35(3).

case_name: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / Mandatory FIR Registration
ratio_decidendi: Registration of an FIR under Section 154 CrPC (now Section 173 BNSS) is mandatory if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. Police have no discretion to conduct a preliminary inquiry when cognizable allegations are made.
key_principles: If information discloses a cognizable offence, no preliminary inquiry is permissible and FIR must be registered immediately.
Preliminary inquiry is permissible only in limited exceptions: matrimonial disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence, corruption cases, or cases with abnormal delay.
Any preliminary inquiry must be completed within 14 days (tightened by subsequent directives to 7 days).
Action must be taken against erring police officers who refuse to register an FIR disclosing a cognizable offence.
currentness_check: Reenacted with express statutory recognition in Section 173(3) BNSS 2023, which codifies preliminary inquiry parameters for offences punishable between 3 and 7 years while preserving mandatory registration for serious crimes.

case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / Anticipatory Bail
ratio_decidendi: The power to grant anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC (now Section 482 BNSS) is of wide amplitude and anchored in personal liberty under Article 21. Courts should not read narrow restrictions into the provision that Parliament did not enact.
key_principles: Anticipatory bail cannot be refused merely because an accusation of a serious non-bailable offence is leveled.
Filing of an FIR is not a condition precedent for invoking anticipatory bail jurisdiction.
The court must balance the personal liberty of the applicant against the legitimate needs of police investigation.
Anticipatory bail orders should not be made overly restrictive or limited in duration unless specific circumstances require it.
currentness_check: Affirmed as foundational constitutional jurisprudence by the 5-judge Constitution Bench in Sushila Aggarwal (2020) 5 SCC 1 and binding under BNSS 2023 Section 482.

case_name: Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi)
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / Anticipatory Bail Duration
ratio_decidendi: Anticipatory bail granted under Section 438 CrPC (BNSS Section 482) is not normally limited to a fixed time period and can continue till the conclusion of trial, unless special circumstances warrant a time-limited grant.
key_principles: Protection of anticipatory bail does not automatically expire upon the filing of a chargesheet.
Courts can impose tailored conditions to ensure cooperation with investigation, but cannot impose blanket expiry dates.
Police can apply for cancellation of bail under Section 439(2) CrPC (BNSS Section 483(3)) if terms are breached or custodial interrogation becomes genuinely essential.
currentness_check: Current authoritative 5-Judge Constitution Bench precedent governing anticipatory bail under BNSS Section 482.

case_name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
legal_domain: Law of Evidence / Electronic Records Admissibility
ratio_decidendi: A certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act (now Section 63(4) Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023) is a mandatory condition precedent for the admissibility of secondary electronic records (CDs, printouts, pendrives, mobile screenshots). Overruled Tomaso Bruno and clarified Shafhi Mohammad.
key_principles: Production of the original electronic device/storage medium dispenses with certificate requirement (primary evidence under Section 62 IEA / Section 57 BSA).
Any reproduction or printout from an electronic source is secondary evidence and strictly inadmissible without a statutory certificate.
Trial courts have power under Section 91 CrPC (Section 94 BNSS) and Section 165 Evidence Act to summon certificates before conclusion of trial.
currentness_check: Binding precedent directly governing electronic evidence admissibility under Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 Section 63 (which reenacts Section 65B with updated schedule forms).

case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
legal_domain: Constitutional Law / Fundamental Right to Privacy
ratio_decidendi: Privacy is a fundamental right protected intrinsically as part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as an aspect of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. Overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) to the extent they held privacy was not a fundamental right.
key_principles: Right to privacy encompasses informational privacy, bodily integrity, and spatial privacy.

Any state encroachment on privacy must satisfy the three-fold proportionality test: (1) Legality (statutory law), (2) Legitimate state aim, and (3) Proportionality (suitability, necessity, and least intrusive means).
Protects citizens against unauthorized digital surveillance, data scraping, and invasive bodily tests.
currentness_check: Highest-bench constitutional authority (9 judges). Formed the constitutional bedrock for the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDPA).

case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
legal_domain: Constitutional Law / Substantive Due Process
ratio_decidendi: Procedure established by law under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive; it must be 'right, just, and fair'. Articles 14, 19, and 21 form an organic golden triangle and cannot be read in isolated watertight compartments.
key_principles: Natural justice (audi alteram partem) is an essential component of administrative and penal procedures affecting personal liberty.
Impounding a passport or restricting travel without giving a post-decisional or pre-decisional hearing violates Article 21.
Transformed Indian constitutional law from strict formal procedure to substantive fairness and reasonableness.
currentness_check: Pillar of Indian constitutional jurisprudence; continuously cited and applied across all fundamental rights litigation.

case_name: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / Comprehensive Bail Guidelines
ratio_decidendi: Reiterated that 'bail is the rule and jail is the exception.' Formulated a 4-category classification of offences (Category A to D) to streamline bail adjudications without routine arrest and detention for undertrials.
key_principles: Category A (offences punishable up to 7 years): No arrest should be made if accused complied with Section 41A notices; bail should be granted on appearance without police custody.
Category B (heinous offences): Bail decided on merits of chargesheet and gravity.
Category C (special acts like NDPS, PMLA, POCSO): Bail decided subject to statutory negative conditions.
Category D (economic offences): Bail considered taking into account systemic financial impact.
Strict compliance with Section 41 and 41A CrPC is mandatory; non-compliance entitles accused to immediate bail.
currentness_check: Actively enforced by the Supreme Court as a continuing mandamus matter with compliance monitoring across all State High Courts and subordinate judiciaries; fully applies under BNSS 2023.

case_name: Aparna Bhat v. State of Madhya Pradesh
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / Bail Conditions in Gender Crimes
ratio_decidendi: Courts must not impose bail conditions that reinforce gender stereotypes, demean the victim, or seek compromise between accused and victim in sexual offence cases. Quashed High Court condition directing accused to get rakhi tied by victim.
key_principles: Bail conditions must strictly relate to ensuring presence at trial and preventing tampering with evidence.
No bail condition should require contact between accused and victim or require mediation/compromise in sexual offences.
Judicial orders must remain sensitive, gender-neutral, and strictly within statutory parameters.
currentness_check: Mandatory precedent across all criminal trials involving POCSO, BNS Section 74 (assault on women), and domestic violence cases.

case_name: P. Mohanraj v. Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd.
legal_domain: Commercial Criminal Law / Section 138 Cheque Bounce & Insolvency
ratio_decidendi: Proceedings under Section 138 and Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are quasi-criminal in nature and fall squarely within the scope of the statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).
key_principles: Cheque bounce proceedings against the corporate debtor are stayed during the CIRP moratorium period.
The moratorium under Section 14 IBC does not shield natural person directors, signatories, or promoters, who remain personally liable to face Section 138 prosecution.
Harmonized commercial debt resolution with criminal statutory protections.
currentness_check: Authoritative ruling on interaction between Negotiable Instruments Act and IBC moratoriums.

case_name: M/s Meters and Instruments Pvt. Ltd. v. Kanchan Mehta
legal_domain: Commercial Criminal Law / Compounding of Cheque Bounce
ratio_decidendi: Section 138 NI Act is primarily a civil wrong for enforcing recovery of debt dressed in criminal clothes. The court has power under Section 147 NI Act to compound the offence and discharge the accused upon deposit of the cheque amount plus reasonable costs, even without the complainant's consent.
key_principles: The object of Section 138 is recovery of money, not incarceration of the drawer.
If the accused makes full compensatory payment and reasonable interest/costs as determined by the magistrate, proceedings may be closed.
Promotes decongestion of magistrate courts handling massive cheque bounce backlogs.
currentness_check: Reaffirmed in Expeditious Trial of Cases under Section 138 NI Act, In re (2021) SCC OnLine SC 325 by a 5-judge Constitution Bench.

case_name: Social Action Forum for Manav Adhikar v. Union of India
legal_domain: Matrimonial Criminal Law / Section 498A Cruelty
ratio_decidendi: Modified the previous directions in Rajesh Sharma v. State of U.P. (2017). Quashed the creation of extra-statutory 'Family Welfare Committees' because creating pre-FIR mediation committees with no statutory foundation curtailed police investigations and victim access to justice under Section 498A IPC.
key_principles: Family Welfare Committees cannot act as gatekeepers to statutory criminal complaints.
The safeguards against arbitrary arrest are already adequately provided under Section 41 and 41A CrPC as interpreted in Arnesh Kumar.
Restored direct statutory procedure while affirming the availability of anticipatory bail.
currentness_check: Modified earlier ruling in Rajesh Sharma. Binding current law on matrimonial cruelty prosecutions under BNS 2023 Section 85/86 and BNSS Section 35.

case_name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
legal_domain: Constitutional Law / Decriminalization of Consensual Acts
ratio_decidendi: Section 377 IPC, insofar as it criminalized consensual sexual acts between consenting adults in private, violated Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 of the Constitution. Overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation (2014).
key_principles: Constitutional morality prevails over majoritarian social or religious morality.
Sexual orientation is an inherent attribute of human dignity and identity protected under Article 21.
Non-consensual acts and acts against minors remain criminal offences.
currentness_check: Statutorily reflected in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, where Section 377 IPC has been omitted entirely. Non-consensual sexual offenses are governed under BNS rape and assault provisions.

case_name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
legal_domain: Constitutional Law / Striking Down Adultery Offence
ratio_decidendi: Section 497 IPC (adultery) was struck down as unconstitutional for treating women as chattel and property of their husbands, violating Articles 14, 15, and 21. Adultery may remain a civil ground for divorce but cannot be a criminal offence.
key_principles: Criminalizing marital infidelity discriminates against women and infringes personal autonomy and privacy.
Section 198(2) CrPC was also struck down insofar as it prevented the wife from prosecuting or being prosecuted.
The State has no legitimate business policing consensual adult relationships inside matrimony via the penal code.
currentness_check: Statutorily consolidated: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does not contain any offence of adultery.

case_name: Youth Bar Association of India v. Union of India
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / Public Transparency of FIRs
ratio_decidendi: To safeguard accused persons' constitutional rights under Article 21, copies of registered FIRs must be uploaded on state police websites within 24 to 72 hours of registration, enabling timely legal recourse and bail applications.
key_principles: FIR copies must be uploaded within 24 hours of registration, extendable up to 48 or 72 hours in remote or hilly terrains.
Exemption is granted for sensitive cases (rape, sexual offences, terrorism, insurgency) to protect victim identity and public safety.
Accused or their representative is entitled to receive an official copy of the FIR within 24 hours of applying.
currentness_check: Reenacted in spirit under BNSS 2023 Section 173(1), which mandates digital registration and forwarding of FIR copies to magistrates and complainants.

case_name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
legal_domain: Constitutional Criminal Law / Self-Incrimination & Scientific Interrogation
ratio_decidendi: Involuntary administration of neuroscientific investigative techniques (narco-analysis, polygraph / lie-detector, and Brain Electrical Activation Profile / BEAP) violates the privilege against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and the right to privacy and bodily integrity under Article 21.
key_principles: No individual can be compelled to undergo narco-analysis or lie detector tests without voluntary and informed consent.
Even when administered voluntarily with legal counsel present, test results themselves cannot be admitted as substantive evidence.
Subsequent physical facts or materials discovered as a result of voluntary statements may be admitted under Section 27 Evidence Act (now Section 23 BSA 2023).
currentness_check: Settled landmark law safeguarding accused against coercive scientific interrogation under Article 20(3) and BSA Section 23.

case_name: Common Cause v. Union of India
legal_domain: Constitutional Law / Passive Euthanasia & Living Wills
ratio_decidendi: The right to life with dignity under Article 21 includes the right to die with dignity and to refuse life-prolonging invasive medical treatment. Recognized the legal validity of Advance Medical Directives (Living Wills) and passive euthanasia.
key_principles: An adult of sound mind has the legal right to execute an Advance Medical Directive specifying medical treatment refusal in vegetative/terminal states.
Strict safeguards and two-tier medical boards (Hospital Primary Medical Board and Review Medical Board) are mandated.
Guidelines were further simplified and streamlined by the Supreme Court in its January 2023 miscellaneous order.
currentness_check: Landmark 5-Judge Constitution Bench decision; procedures refined in 2023 order to make execution before notaries/gazetted officers simpler.

case_name: Dr. Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra
legal_domain: Special Criminal Acts / SC/ST Act Arrest Guidelines
ratio_decidendi: Imposed preliminary inquiry by DSP and prior sanction/approval requirements before arresting public servants or private citizens under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
key_principles: Required preliminary inquiry within 7 days before registering an FIR.
Required prior written approval of the appointing authority or SSP before arresting an accused.
Held that anticipatory bail could be granted despite Section 18 bar if no prima facie case was made out.
currentness_check: SUPERSEDED & NULLIFIED: Parliament enacted the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Amendment Act, 2018 (Act 27 of 2018), inserting Section 18A on 17 August 2018, which explicitly eliminated preliminary inquiry and prior approval requirements. The 3-judge review bench of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. State of Maharashtra (2020) 4 SCC 761 and Constitution Bench in Prathvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020) 4 SCC 727 formally recalled the Mahajan directions and upheld Section 18A.

case_name: T.T. Antony v. State of Kerala
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / Bar Against Second FIR
ratio_decidendi: There can be no second FIR, nor can there be a fresh investigation, in respect of the same cognizable offence or same occurrence/transaction. Any further information received by police must be treated as a statement during investigation under Section 162 CrPC or further investigation under Section 173(8) CrPC.
key_principles: A second FIR on the same incident amounts to abuse of process and is liable to be quashed.
The 'Sameness Test': if gravamen of both FIRs relates to the same transaction, subsequent FIR is prohibited.
Cross-FIRs or rival counter-versions of an incident are permissible exceptions.
currentness_check: Reaffirmed by 3-judge bench in Babubhai v. State of Gujarat (2010) 12 SCC 254 and Anju Chaudhary (2013). Fully binding under BNSS Section 173 & Section 193(9).

case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
legal_domain: Criminal Procedure / High Court Quashing of FIRs
ratio_decidendi: Formulated the definitive 7 illustrative categories where the High Court can exercise its inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC (now Section 528 BNSS) or extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to quash an FIR or criminal complaint to prevent abuse of process of court.
key_principles: Category 1: Where allegations in the FIR, even if taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute any offence.
Category 2: Where allegations are so absurd and inherently improbable that no prudent person can reach a conclusion of sufficient ground for proceeding.
Category 3: Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any Act to the institution or continuance of proceedings.
Category 4: Where criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fides or maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance.
currentness_check: The universal bedrock precedent cited in every Section 482 CrPC / Section 528 BNSS petition across every High Court in India.
